title: Asset Inventory: Prerequisite for All Security

blocks.text: You can only protect what you know exists. A forgotten asset is unpatched, unmonitored, and unrestored. Objective 4.2 is less about tools than about **inventory discipline**.
Hardware, Software, Data: Three Asset Categories

blocks.note: Asset Management chapter: inventorying hardware, software, and data

head: Category
Examples
Risk If Uninventoried
rows: Servers, workstations, mobile devices, network equipment

blocks.field: Registry of assets with owner, location, version, criticality, and status. It feeds patching, incident response, and recovery.

blocks.note: Knowing what you are protecting and why: composite inventory

blocks.text: A **composite inventory** is not just a list of machines: it links the asset to its **owner**, its **business criticality**, the **data** it processes, and the **dependencies** it relies on. That relationship is what enables proper remediation prioritization.
When a scenario mentions an unpatched "forgotten server" at the root of a breach, the root cause is almost always **lack of inventory** (including shadow IT).
What an Asset Record Should Contain

items: Unique identifier, type, make/model, and serial number.
Owner and custodian: who decides and who operates.
Software version, patch level, end-of-support date.
Classification of processed data and business criticality.
Lifecycle status and planned decommissioning date.

blocks.q: An unlisted server exposes an old version of an application. What is the most likely root cause?
options: Lack of inventory and lifecycle tracking
blocks.explain: An uninventoried asset escapes patching, monitoring, and end-of-life controls: this is an asset management failure.

items: Hardware, software, and data must all be inventoried.
A composite inventory links asset, owner, criticality, and dependencies.
Without inventory: no targeted patching, no effective response, no reliable recovery.
The asset record follows the equipment through decommissioning.

title: The Lifecycle: From Acquisition to Decommissioning

blocks.text: The objectives describe a staged lifecycle: **planning, acquisition, assignment, monitoring, decommissioning**. Each stage introduces specific security controls — and the final stage is often the most neglected.

items.title: Planning / scoping
items.text: Define the need, criticality, security requirements, and expected lifespan before any purchase.

items.title: Acquisition / procurement
items.text: Build security requirements into the specification: encryption, support, compliance, end-of-life terms.

items.title: Assignment / accounting
items.text: Assign an owner, record the asset in inventory, label it, and document authorized use.

items.title: Monitoring / asset tracking
items.text: Track status, patches, movements, and usage; detect ghost assets and shadow IT.

items.title: Disposal / decommissioning
items.text: Wipe or destroy data, revoke access, and certify the asset's end of life.

blocks.field: Final lifecycle process: wiping or destroying media, revoking access and licenses, then obtaining certified proof of the asset's end of life.

blocks.text: Security requirements must be written **before** purchase: support duration, guaranteed updates, native encryption, certified erasure capability. Assignment creates accountability: without a named owner, no one monitors the asset.

blocks.note: Tracking, hardening, and managing acquired systems

blocks.text: Tracking combines passive inventory (network discovery, MDM, CMDB) and active checks (periodic reviews). A discrepancy between inventory and reality signals **shadow IT** or a rogue device to investigate.
Decommissioning: The Stage That Leaks Most

items: Secure erasure or physical destruction of media.
Revocation of associated accounts, certificates, tokens, and licenses.
Retention of evidence and certificate of destruction.
Compliance with legal retention periods before erasure.

blocks.note: Tracking and end-of-life handling of equipment

blocks.text: A disk leaving the company without certified erasure is a data leak. Decommissioning must always produce **proof**: certificate of destruction or erasure report.

blocks.q: In what order should you proceed for new equipment?
blocks.explain: Planning → acquisition → assignment/inventory → tracking → decommissioning. Purchasing without planning or an owner escapes all control.

items: Plan, acquire, assign, track, decommission: five ordered stages.
Security requirements are written into specifications before purchase.
Every asset receives an owner and an inventory identifier.
Decommissioning requires certified erasure, access revocation, and proof of destruction.
